The Virginia opossum (Didelphis virginiana) exhibits a remarkably rapid life history among marsupials, with field records indicating that females reach sexual maturity at approximately 184 days after birth [tp = approximately 184 days after birth] under typical thermal conditions of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This swift maturation is complemented by an exceptionally short gestation period of only 12.5 days [tg = 12.5 days] at the same temperature, among the briefest documented for any mammal at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. The neonates emerging from this abbreviated uterine development are profoundly altricial, weighing a mere 0.147 grams [Wwb = 0.147 grams] at birth. This minuscule birth mass, comparable to a grain of rice, reflects the marsupial strategy of giving birth to highly underdeveloped young that complete most of their development while attached to a teat within the pouch. The total length of this species, measured from the tip of the nose to the end of the tail, typically reaches an ultimate value of 33 centimeters [Li = 33 centimeters], though individuals ranging from 21.6 to 47 centimeters have been documented across its expansive geographic range.

Lactation and pouch life represent a critical phase of development for the altricial neonates, and under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 35 °C [T = 35 °C], the time since birth at weaning has been recorded as 102 days [tx = 102 days]. At this developmental milestone, the young opossums, having spent weeks firmly attached to a teat, achieve a wet weight at weaning of 142.5 grams [Wwx = 142.5 grams], representing a nearly thousand-fold increase from their neonatal mass. This dramatic growth trajectory is sustained entirely by the mother's milk, placing a substantial energetic demand on the lactating female. The extended period of pouch residence and subsequent nursing distinguishes the opossum from many eutherian mammals of similar body size, though it is typical of didelphid marsupials. Following weaning, the young individuals transition to a solitary, omnivorous foraging strategy, rapidly acquiring the skills necessary to exploit the diverse array of food resources available in their environment, from insects and carrion to fruits and small vertebrates.

Significant sexual dimorphism in body mass is a prominent feature of Virginia opossum biology, with the ultimate wet weight for females averaging approximately 3000 grams [Wwi = approximately 3000 grams], while males achieve a considerably larger ultimate wet weight of 6000 grams [Wwi = 6000 grams]. This twofold difference in adult body mass is thought to be driven by sexual selection, where larger males enjoy a competitive advantage during the breeding season. The maximum recorded longevity for this species, when maintained under optimal captive conditions at a constant temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], is approximately 6.6 years [am = approximately 6.6 years], a relatively short lifespan for a mammal of this size that reflects the species' fast-paced life history strategy. In wild populations, however, mortality is considerably higher due to predation, vehicle collisions, and harsh winter conditions, with very few individuals surviving beyond two or three years, underscoring the disconnect between physiological potential and ecological reality.

The reproductive output of the Virginia opossum is exceptionally high, a strategy that compensates for its short lifespan and high juvenile mortality. Each litter can contain up to 13 young [N_R_i = Each litter can contain up to 13 young], and females produce a maximum of approximately 2.3 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.3 litters per year], yielding a maximum annual reproductive output of approximately 30 young per year [Ri = approximately 30 young per year] under favorable conditions at 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This remarkable fecundity, when assessed as a daily reproductive rate, represents one of the highest among North American mammals and allows the species to rapidly colonize vacant habitats. The constraint of only 13 teats in the pouch imposes a physiological limit on litter size, as any young born beyond this number cannot successfully nurse and will not survive. Mature males reach puberty at a later age than females, with the time since birth at puberty for males recorded at 243 days [tp = 243 days], a delay that likely reflects the extended period required to attain their substantially larger adult body mass.

Comparative studies across didelphid marsupials reveal that the Virginia opossum occupies a fast-living extreme of the life history continuum, characterized by its short gestation of 12.5 days [tg = 12.5 days] and abbreviated lifespan at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. While the breeding adult mammal invests heavily in a single reproductive season through multiple large litters, individual offspring receive minimal parental investment beyond lactation, a trade-off that is reflected in the small 0.147 gram [Wwb = 0.147 gram] neonates. Despite the high potential fecundity, population densities remain relatively stable, regulated by density-dependent factors such as food availability and predation pressure. The Virginia opossum thus exemplifies a high-risk, high-reward reproductive strategy that has enabled its successful expansion across much of North America.
